label: Evaluating Foundation Model Performance — Part A

questions.scenario: A QA team runs the same summarization prompt 5 times against their FM and gets 5 different summaries. All are grammatically correct and factually accurate, but they vary in structure, emphasis, and word choice.
questions.stem: What fundamental characteristic of generative AI makes evaluation more difficult than traditional ML?

options.text: Generative models are too slow to evaluate at scale
Output is non-deterministic — the same input can produce multiple valid outputs, making it impossible to compare against a single ground truth
Generative models cannot produce text longer than 100 tokens
Traditional ML models never require evaluation

explanation.correct: Generative AI outputs are non-deterministic — multiple valid outputs exist for any input. Unlike classification where there's one correct label, summarization has many acceptable variations, requiring task-specific evaluation metrics rather than simple accuracy.

distractors.A: Speed is an operational concern, not a fundamental evaluation challenge. Evaluation difficulty stems from output variability, not throughput.
distractors.C: Modern models generate thousands of tokens. The challenge is measuring quality of diverse valid outputs, not output length.
distractors.D: All ML models require evaluation. Traditional models are simpler to evaluate because predictions can be directly compared to deterministic ground truth.

questions.scenario: A news organization deploys an FM to summarize articles. They need an automated metric to evaluate how well generated summaries capture the key information from source articles by comparing against human-written reference summaries.
questions.stem: Which metric is specifically designed for this summarization evaluation task?

options.text: BLEU — measures precision of n-gram overlap with reference translations
BERTScore — measures deep semantic similarity using contextual embeddings
ROUGE — measures recall of n-gram overlap between generated and reference summaries, capturing how much reference content is preserved
Perplexity — measures how surprised the model is by a sequence of tokens

explanation.correct: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) evaluates automatic summarization by measuring what proportion of reference summary content appears in the generated summary. Its recall-focus captures information coverage.

distractors.A: BLEU is precision-focused and designed for translation evaluation. While it uses n-gram overlap, it optimizes for different characteristics than summarization requires.
distractors.B: BERTScore measures semantic similarity but isn't the established standard for summarization evaluation. ROUGE is the canonical summarization metric.
distractors.D: Perplexity measures language modeling quality (how well the model predicts text). It doesn't compare generated output against reference summaries.

questions.scenario: A translation team evaluates their English-to-Japanese model. They compare generated translations against professional human translations to measure how much of the machine translation matches the reference.
questions.stem: Which metric is the established standard for evaluating machine translation quality?

options.text: ROUGE — recall-oriented metric for summarization tasks
BLEU — measures precision of n-gram overlap between machine-generated translations and human reference translations
MMLU — tests world knowledge across academic domains
HELM — holistic model evaluation across multiple dimensions

explanation.correct: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is the standard metric for machine translation. It measures precision — what proportion of n-grams in the generated translation also appear in reference human translations.

distractors.A: ROUGE evaluates summarization with a recall focus. Translation evaluation requires precision-focused metrics like BLEU.
distractors.C: MMLU is a benchmark for testing knowledge breadth, not a metric for evaluating translation quality.
distractors.D: HELM evaluates model capabilities holistically across tasks. It's a benchmark framework, not a translation-specific metric.

questions.scenario: A team evaluates their RAG-based QA system. They need a metric that captures whether generated answers are semantically faithful to source documents — even when the model paraphrases rather than copying exact words.
questions.stem: Which metric evaluates semantic similarity rather than exact word overlap?

options.text: ROUGE-1 — counts matching unigrams between generated and reference text
Exact match — checks if generated text is identical to the reference
Word error rate — counts the number of word-level edits needed to transform one text into another
BERTScore — uses contextual embeddings to measure semantic similarity, capturing meaning preservation even when wording differs

explanation.correct: BERTScore computes similarity using contextual embeddings from pre-trained language models. It captures semantic equivalence between paraphrases that share meaning but differ in surface form — ideal for evaluating faithfulness without requiring exact word matches.

distractors.A: ROUGE-1 counts matching individual words. It misses semantic similarity when the model paraphrases with different vocabulary.
distractors.B: Exact match fails when any word differs, even if the meaning is perfectly preserved through paraphrasing.
distractors.C: Word error rate measures edit distance, penalizing paraphrases that preserve meaning but use different words.

questions.scenario: A company wants to compare multiple LLMs on their ability to answer questions about history, mathematics, law, biology, and computer science — testing breadth of world knowledge across academic disciplines.
questions.stem: Which benchmark specifically evaluates world knowledge across diverse academic domains?

options.text: MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) — tests knowledge across dozens of academic subjects from STEM to humanities
GLUE — tests basic language understanding tasks like sentiment and textual entailment
BLEU — evaluates translation quality against references
BIG-bench — tests tasks beyond current model capabilities

explanation.correct: MMLU tests models across dozens of academic subjects including history, math, law, biology, medicine, and computer science. It specifically evaluates breadth of world knowledge and problem-solving across disciplines.

distractors.B: GLUE tests standard NLP tasks (sentiment, similarity) — language understanding, not world knowledge across academic fields.
distractors.C: BLEU is a single metric for translation quality. It doesn't test knowledge breadth across subjects.
distractors.D: BIG-bench tests challenging capabilities but includes diverse tasks. MMLU is specifically designed for academic world knowledge evaluation.

questions.stem: Which are established benchmarks for evaluating LLM capabilities? (Select THREE)

options.text: GLUE/SuperGLUE — standard language understanding tasks including reasoning and reading comprehension
HELM — holistic evaluation combining metrics across summarization, Q&A, sentiment, and bias with task-specific guidance
BIG-bench — tasks beyond current model capabilities including math, physics, and reasoning
SPEED-INDEX — measuring model inference throughput per dollar
COST-RANK — comparing deployment expenses across cloud providers
MEM-SCORE — measuring GPU memory utilization efficiency

explanation.correct: GLUE/SuperGLUE evaluates language understanding, HELM provides holistic evaluation with task-specific guidance and transparency, and BIG-bench tests capabilities beyond current model limits. These are recognized research benchmarks.

distractors.D: No standard benchmark called SPEED-INDEX exists. Throughput is an operational metric measured per deployment, not a capability benchmark.
distractors.E: COST-RANK is not a real benchmark. Cost comparison is a business decision, not a model capability evaluation.
distractors.F: MEM-SCORE is not an established benchmark. Memory utilization is an infrastructure metric unrelated to model quality evaluation.

questions.scenario: A team deploys their LLM and finds it exceeds their latency budget. They explore optimization approaches.
questions.stem: Which techniques can reduce inference latency? (Select THREE)

options.text: Reduce model size through quantization or distillation — smaller models load and process faster
Make prompts more concise — fewer input tokens means less processing time
Reduce the size and number of retrieved snippets in RAG pipelines — less context processing per request
Increase model parameters to improve inference speed through parallelism
Add more layers to the model architecture during deployment
Increase temperature to make the model generate tokens faster

explanation.correct: Smaller models process faster (fewer computations), shorter prompts reduce input processing time, and fewer RAG snippets reduce context length. All may trade some quality for improved latency.

distractors.D: More parameters increase computation per forward pass, increasing latency. Parallelism helps throughput but not per-request latency.
distractors.E: Adding layers increases computation depth, making inference slower. Architecture changes at deployment time aren't standard practice.
distractors.F: Temperature affects token selection strategy, not processing speed. It controls randomness, not computational efficiency.

questions.scenario: A team needs to evaluate and compare multiple foundation models for their use case using both automated metrics and human judgment.
questions.stem: What capabilities does Amazon SageMaker Clarify provide for FM evaluation? (Select TWO)

options.text: Creates model evaluation jobs to evaluate and compare quality metrics for text-based FMs from JumpStart
Supports human workers to manually evaluate and compare model responses alongside automated metrics
Automatically selects the best model and deploys it to production without human review
Generates synthetic training data to augment fine-tuning datasets
Provides real-time inference endpoints for production traffic

explanation.correct: SageMaker Clarify creates evaluation jobs for comparing FM quality metrics and supports human workers for manual response comparison — providing both automated and human evaluation workflows.

distractors.C: Clarify evaluates and compares but doesn't auto-deploy. Model selection and deployment decisions remain with the team.
distractors.D: Data generation is a different capability. Clarify focuses on evaluation, not training data creation.
distractors.E: Inference endpoints are provided by SageMaker Hosting, not Clarify. Clarify is specifically for evaluation and bias analysis.

questions.scenario: A company deploys a generative AI assistant and needs to determine whether it meets their business objectives.
questions.stem: What must they establish to evaluate business success of their gen AI deployment? (Select THREE)

options.text: Define specific business goals the AI should achieve (productivity improvement, user engagement, cost reduction)
Determine measurable metrics that indicate whether goals are being met
Continuously monitor and review metrics to track performance over time
Only measure the model's BLEU score as the sole indicator of business value
Compare model parameter count against competitors as the primary success metric
Count the number of API calls as the only metric regardless of outcome quality

explanation.correct: Business evaluation requires defined goals (what to achieve), measurable success metrics (how to know if goals are met), and continuous monitoring (tracking over time). Technical metrics alone don't capture business value.

distractors.D: BLEU measures translation quality — a technical metric unrelated to business outcomes like productivity or engagement.
distractors.E: Parameter count is a model characteristic. Business success is measured by outcomes delivered, not model architecture comparisons.
distractors.F: API call volume measures usage but not value. High usage with poor quality doesn't constitute business success.

questions.stem: Why is human evaluation important alongside automated metrics for LLM assessment? (Select TWO)

options.text: Automated metrics like ROUGE and BLEU capture surface-level features but may miss nuances in quality, helpfulness, and safety that humans can assess
Human evaluators can compare responses from multiple models side-by-side, assessing subjective qualities like tone, clarity, and usefulness
Human evaluation is free and requires no infrastructure
Automated metrics are always wrong and should never be used
Human evaluation eliminates all subjectivity from the assessment process

explanation.correct: Automated metrics capture quantifiable features but miss subjective quality dimensions. Human evaluators assess nuanced qualities (tone, helpfulness, safety) and can compare multiple model outputs holistically.

distractors.C: Human evaluation requires recruiting, training, and compensating evaluators. It has significant time and cost implications.
distractors.D: Automated metrics are useful for scalable, reproducible measurement. They complement human evaluation — neither alone is sufficient.
distractors.E: Human evaluation introduces subjectivity (different evaluators may disagree). Its value is capturing nuances, not eliminating subjectivity.

questions.scenario: A company deploys their LLM to mobile devices with 4GB RAM and strict 200ms latency requirements. The full model requires 16GB and takes 800ms per completion.
questions.stem: What tradeoff must they accept when reducing model size to meet these constraints?

options.text: Smaller models always produce identical quality to larger models
Reduced model size decreases memory usage and latency but may decrease accuracy and response quality
Model size reduction only affects storage cost, not inference quality
The only way to meet latency constraints is to switch to a rule-based system

explanation.correct: Reducing model size (through distillation, quantization, or pruning) decreases memory and latency but typically reduces accuracy. This is the fundamental optimization tradeoff — speed and efficiency vs model performance.

distractors.A: Smaller models generally have lower quality due to fewer parameters capturing less complex patterns. Quality reduction is the tradeoff.
distractors.C: Size directly affects inference speed (fewer computations) and quality (fewer parameters). It impacts far more than just storage.
distractors.D: Model optimization techniques (quantization, distillation) can meet latency constraints while preserving ML capabilities.

questions.scenario: A research team needs a benchmark that provides transparency about model capabilities and offers guidance on which specific model performs best for particular tasks like summarization, Q&A, and sentiment analysis.
questions.stem: Which benchmark provides this holistic evaluation with task-specific guidance?

options.text: MMLU — tests factual knowledge across academic domains
BIG-bench — challenges models with tasks beyond current capabilities
GLUE — tests basic NLP tasks with a single aggregate score
HELM (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models) — improves model transparency and provides per-task guidance on model selection

explanation.correct: HELM evaluates models holistically across multiple dimensions (summarization, Q&A, sentiment, bias) and provides transparency about strengths and weaknesses — offering guidance on which model performs best for specific tasks.

distractors.A: MMLU tests knowledge breadth but doesn't provide per-task model selection guidance or holistic transparency across diverse evaluation dimensions.
distractors.B: BIG-bench focuses on challenging frontier tasks. It doesn't provide the per-task guidance for practical model selection that HELM offers.
distractors.C: GLUE tests standard NLP tasks but produces aggregate scores rather than the detailed per-task transparency and guidance HELM provides.

questions.scenario: A team evaluates two LLMs for their customer support chatbot. Model A scores higher on ROUGE and BLEU but users consistently prefer Model B's responses in A/B tests, rating them as more helpful and natural.
questions.stem: What does this discrepancy reveal about LLM evaluation?

options.text: The automated metrics must be calculated incorrectly since users always agree with metrics
User preferences are unreliable and should be ignored in favor of automated metrics
Model B must have been fine-tuned while Model A was not, explaining the preference gap
Automated metrics capture surface-level text features but may not align with human perception of quality, helpfulness, and naturalness — both evaluation types provide complementary insights

explanation.correct: Automated metrics measure quantifiable text properties (n-gram overlap, similarity scores) but don't capture subjective qualities humans value (helpfulness, naturalness, tone). The discrepancy shows both metrics and human evaluation are needed for comprehensive assessment.

distractors.A: Metrics and human preferences can legitimately diverge because they measure different aspects of quality.
distractors.B: User preferences are the ultimate measure of product quality for customer-facing applications. Dismissing them ignores real-world value.
distractors.C: Training approach is speculative. The point is that metrics and human judgment measure different quality dimensions regardless of how models were built.

questions.stem: ROUGE-L measures the longest common subsequence between generated and reference text. A summary that restructures sentences while preserving all key information would score differently on ROUGE-1 vs ROUGE-L. Why?

options.text: ROUGE-1 counts individual word overlap regardless of order; ROUGE-L captures sequential structure — restructured text preserves words (high ROUGE-1) but changes their sequence (potentially lower ROUGE-L)
ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-L always produce identical scores for any text
ROUGE-L only works for translations, not summaries
ROUGE-1 measures semantic meaning while ROUGE-L measures grammar

explanation.correct: ROUGE-1 counts unigram overlap (order-independent) while ROUGE-L finds the longest common subsequence (order-sensitive). Restructured text with the same words but different order can score high on ROUGE-1 but lower on ROUGE-L.

distractors.B: They measure different properties and routinely produce different scores. Order-sensitive and order-independent metrics capture different aspects.
distractors.C: ROUGE-L works for any text comparison task, including summarization. It measures sequential similarity regardless of the generation task.
distractors.D: Neither measures semantic meaning directly. ROUGE-1 counts word overlap; ROUGE-L measures subsequence alignment. Both are surface-level metrics.

questions.scenario: An architect designs the deployment stack for a generative AI application. They need to plan infrastructure, model selection, user interface, and security.
questions.stem: Which layer of the gen AI application stack determines what LLMs to use and how inference will be served?

options.text: The infrastructure layer — compute, storage, and networking
The user interface layer — how end users interact with the application
The security layer — authentication and access control
The model layer — choosing LLMs and configuring appropriate infrastructure for inference requirements

explanation.correct: The model layer determines which foundation models to use and ensures appropriate infrastructure for their inference requirements (GPU types, memory, throughput). It bridges between infrastructure capabilities and application needs.

distractors.A: Infrastructure provides the compute/storage/network resources. The model layer makes decisions about which models to deploy on that infrastructure.
distractors.B: The UI layer handles user interaction. Model selection and inference configuration are backend decisions in the model layer.
distractors.C: Security spans all layers. Model selection is a technical capability decision, not a security concern (though security applies to it).

questions.scenario: A solutions architect plans the complete gen AI application stack for an enterprise deployment.
questions.stem: What are key components of the generative AI application stack? (Select THREE)

options.text: Infrastructure layer — compute, storage, and network to serve LLMs and host application components
Model layer — selection of LLMs and appropriate inference infrastructure to meet performance requirements
User interface layer — website or REST API through which the application is consumed by end users
Marketing layer — social media campaigns to promote the AI features
Legal layer — patent filing for each model interaction pattern
Hardware layer — designing custom silicon for each application

explanation.correct: The gen AI stack comprises infrastructure (compute/storage/network), model layer (LLM selection + inference infrastructure), and UI layer (website/API). Security spans all layers.

distractors.D: Marketing is a business function, not a component of the technical application stack architecture.
distractors.E: Patent filing is a legal/IP activity unrelated to the technical deployment architecture.
distractors.F: Custom silicon design is chip engineering. Gen AI applications use existing compute services, not custom hardware per application.

questions.scenario: A team uses Amazon Bedrock to evaluate their foundation model's outputs.
questions.stem: Which evaluation capabilities does Amazon Bedrock provide? (Select TWO)

options.text: Automated evaluation using metrics like BERTScore to measure semantic similarity between generated responses and human references
Model evaluation jobs that compare multiple models available in Bedrock's catalog
Automatic correction of all hallucinated content without human review
Guaranteed elimination of all bias in model outputs
Real-time retraining triggered by low evaluation scores

explanation.correct: Bedrock supports automated evaluation metrics (including BERTScore for semantic similarity and faithfulness) and model comparison jobs. These help teams select the best model for their use case through systematic evaluation.

distractors.C: Evaluation identifies issues but doesn't automatically fix them. Hallucination detection requires separate mitigation strategies.
distractors.D: Evaluation can detect bias but cannot guarantee its elimination. Bias mitigation requires deliberate intervention beyond evaluation.
distractors.E: Evaluation and training are separate processes. Low scores inform decisions but don't trigger automatic retraining.

questions.scenario: A team considers tradeoffs when optimizing their LLM deployment for cost efficiency.
questions.stem: Which actions trade model performance for operational efficiency? (Select TWO)

options.text: Reducing model size through quantization — lower precision decreases memory and compute but may reduce output quality
Reducing prompt length by removing context — less processing per request but potentially less informed responses
Adding more GPU instances — increases cost without reducing performance
Increasing model parameters — larger models use more resources without efficiency gains
Switching to a newer AWS Region — automatically improves model quality

explanation.correct: Quantization trades precision (potential quality loss) for efficiency (less memory/compute). Shorter prompts trade context (less informed responses) for speed (faster processing). Both sacrifice some quality for operational gains.

distractors.C: More GPUs increase cost without trading performance. This is scaling, not optimization through tradeoff.
distractors.D: Increasing parameters worsens efficiency. Optimization trades in the opposite direction — reducing resources while accepting some quality loss.
distractors.E: AWS Region affects latency and data residency but doesn't change model quality or create a performance tradeoff.

questions.scenario: A team needs a benchmark that tests models on challenging tasks intentionally beyond current capabilities — including advanced math, scientific reasoning, and software development problems.
questions.stem: Which benchmark specifically targets tasks beyond the current frontier of model capabilities?

options.text: GLUE — tests standard NLP tasks like sentiment and textual entailment
MMLU — tests world knowledge across academic subjects
BIG-bench (Beyond the Imitation Game) — contains tasks in math, physics, biology, reasoning, and software development that challenge current model limits
ROUGE — measures summarization quality against references

explanation.correct: BIG-bench (Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark) specifically targets tasks beyond current capabilities — including advanced math, scientific reasoning, bias detection, programming, and logical reasoning designed to push model limits.

distractors.A: GLUE tests standard language understanding. Its tasks are within current model capabilities, not beyond them.
distractors.B: MMLU tests knowledge breadth but within established academic content. BIG-bench specifically designs tasks beyond current model limits.
distractors.D: ROUGE is an evaluation metric for summarization, not a benchmark. It measures quality of generated summaries, not model capability limits.

questions.scenario: A company's gen AI chatbot receives positive technical evaluations (high ROUGE scores, good BERTScore) but the business team reports no measurable improvement in customer satisfaction or support ticket resolution time.
questions.stem: What does this indicate about their evaluation approach?

options.text: Technical metrics are sufficient and the business team's measurements must be wrong
The chatbot should be retrained until ROUGE scores are even higher
Technical quality metrics don't guarantee business value — evaluation must include business objective metrics (satisfaction, resolution time) alongside technical metrics
All generative AI deployments fail to deliver business value regardless of technical quality

explanation.correct: Technical quality and business value are different dimensions. High ROUGE/BERTScore means the model generates good text, but business success requires measuring actual impact — customer satisfaction, resolution time, productivity gains. Both must be evaluated.

distractors.A: Technical metrics and business outcomes measure different things. Both can be accurate while showing a disconnect between text quality and business impact.
distractors.B: Higher technical scores won't fix a business value gap. The issue is measuring the wrong thing, not insufficient model quality.
distractors.D: Many gen AI deployments deliver measurable business value. The issue here is incomplete evaluation, not inherent failure of the technology.
